These figures come from GitHub's own production telemetry, which carries vendor credibility caveats but is the authoritative source for platform-level data. The piece explains a specific architectural consequence — the current Spokes design couples durability to read scale, so adding replicas slows writes — and describes the design principles of the replacement (decouple storage from compute via Azure Blob Storage, minimize coordination on the critical write path). An internal benchmark claim of 35x write throughput improvement is presented without reproducible methodology and should be treated as a source claim, not established fact. The post is directly relevant to small teams deciding how to structure agent workflows: high commit-rate agent loops expose latency bottlenecks that humans would not notice, and the described architecture change affects how branching strategies and CI pipelines will behave at scale.     "reason": "This GitHub post announces ReviewBench, an open benchmark for AI code review agents built on 219 pull requests drawn from a 103.9-million-PR distribution analysis across 19 languages. It is directly relevant to the central question: it gives developers a concrete method for evaluating whether a code review agent fits their precision-recall preferences rather than accepting vendor claims. Key methodologically notable claims include: 96.6% agreement between independent senior engineers and the benchmark's golden-set labels; an A/B test where ReviewBench-predicted improvements (8.0% precision gain, 13.6% recall gain, 61% comment volume increase, 8.0% cost reduction) were directionally confirmed in production; and a 227% vs. 262% online critical-comment prediction, showing calibration at severity level. Important limitations to note: this is a GitHub/Microsoft paper about their own product (Copilot Code Review), so the benchmark design, judge choice (Claude Sonnet 5), and validation are all vendor-controlled; the 96.6% agreement figure applies to the dev-set labeling process, not to the benchmark's ability to predict all real-world review quality; the leaderboard is curated by maintainers before publication; and the benchmark corpus excludes tiny single-file PRs by design, which may not match every team's workload. The public availability of the dataset, rubric, judge prompt, and self-serve runner makes independent replication possible, which partially addresses vendor-control concerns. Angle 01 can describe what the benchmark measures and the A/B validation evidence; angle 02 can scrutinize vendor control of the benchmark, the LLM judge choice, and what the benchmark does not cover (e.g., proprietary codebases, accessibility of the review output, smaller teams without resources for container submission); angle 03 can advise teams on how to use the configurable Fβ scoring to match their own review priorities.",
